title: Key squares
summary: Know when king and pawn beat the lone king, and bring your king to the key squares before touching the pawn.
part.keySquares.title: Key squares
part.keySquares.summary: The squares that, once the king stands on one, make sure the pawn queens, whoever is to move.
part.opposition.title: The opposition
part.opposition.summary: With the kings face to face, one square between them and the other side to move, your king climbs from key square to key square up to the sixth rank.
part.defend.title: The defence
part.defend.summary: To defend, the king stays in front of the pawn and steps straight back. That is how Kramnik drew against Kamsky.
step.t_count: The black king is far away, in the corner. Think: where must the white king go so that the e4 pawn is sure to queen, whatever the black king does?
step.t_count.hint1: Don't look at the pawn, look at the squares in front of it. Two ranks ahead, some squares decide everything.
step.intro: Every pawn has key squares. This e4-pawn has three: d6, e6 and f6, two ranks ahead of it. If my king steps on one of them, the pawn queens, whatever the black king does and whoever is to move. The road starts with 1.Ke3, heading for e6. {{Averbakh|yuri-averbakh}} taught that the king leads the pawn the way a father leads his child across the street: he goes in front.
step.count: The count is simple. Pawn up to the fourth rank: three key squares, two ranks ahead. Pawn on the fifth or sixth: six squares, the two ranks ahead, as here with the pawn on e5. On the seventh, the neighbouring squares on the seventh and eighth. With Black the count is the same, downwards: the g5-pawn has f3, g3 and h3. And two pawns have exceptions: the rook pawn, which has a lesson of its own, and the knight pawn, which you will see later.
step.keyWin: Your turn. The king is already on the key square; take the pawn to the seventh rank.
step.keyWin.hint: With the king on e6, the pawn can advance. Then, when the black king gives up one side, take the seventh-rank square on the other side: f7 or d7.
step.keyWin.done: That's it. The pawn reached the seventh with the king beside it. Whoever was to move, the key square won.
step.t_averbakh: The white king is already close, but the black king blocks the way. How does the white king make its way to the sixth rank without touching the pawn?
step.t_averbakh.hint1: The pawn does not have to move. Think about what the black king is forced to do if your king comes right up to him.
step.front: The king is not always on the key square yet. Here the pawn is still on c2, and the key squares are b4, c4 and d4. My king on d4 already holds one of them, but the black king blocks the way. The tool for moving forward is the opposition: kings face to face, one square between them, and the other side to move.
step.tool: Your turn, with another pawn. Take the king to the sixth rank without touching the e2-pawn.
step.tool.hint: First the opposition; when he gives way, go round on the other side.
step.tool.done: Very good. King on the sixth, on d6, and the e2-pawn has not even moved. Now it queens.
step.earlyMove: Your turn, with White. Win with no hurry for the pawn.
step.earlyMove.hint: Not the pawn yet. Take the king to c4 or d4, key squares of the pawn.
step.earlyMove.done: The king got there first and the pawn has not even left d2. With Black it is the same: the king comes down in front of the pawn, towards its key squares.
step.t_kramnik: Now you defend, in a real game. {{Kramnik|vladimir-kramnik}}, with Black, was left with a lone king against king and pawn after a very long rook ending. The white king and pawn look strong. Where must the black king stand so that the pawn never queens?
step.t_kramnik.hint1: Stay on the pawn's file and think of the opposition the other way round: you are the one facing the white king.
step.defend: It was {{Nice|nice}}, 2009, at the {{Amber|melody-amber}} tournament, in a blindfold game, where the players do not see the board: {{Gata Kamsky|gata-kamsky}}, with White, against {{Vladimir Kramnik|vladimir-kramnik}}. The rook ending had been going on since move 69. On move 124, Kamsky blocked a check with his rook on c6, the rooks came off (124...Rxc6+ 125.Kxc6), and Kramnik was left with this position. One wrong step by the black king, and the pawn would queen. To defend, the black king goes in front of the pawn and, when the white king comes up, steps straight back so he can take the opposition.
step.defendMove: Now {{Kramnik|vladimir-kramnik}}'s position. Keep the white king out of the key squares.
step.defendMove.hint: Stay on the pawn's file. When the white king reaches the fifth, in front of the pawn, step back to the eighth; on the seventh he takes the opposition.
step.defendMove.done: That is what {{Kramnik|vladimir-kramnik}} played: 126...Ke8! 127.Kd6 Kd8 128.e7+ Ke8 and 129.Ke6, stalemate. After 126.Kd5, any other square gave away the opposition and the game.
step.recap: To take to your games. Count the key squares and get into one, by any route. The king goes first and the pawn waits; the opposition is the tool. With blocked pawns each king has its own key squares and whoever gets there first wins; if both arrive together, keep a square in reserve and leave the move to him. And for the defender, the mirror image: king in front of the pawn, straight back, and the opposition.
step.finish: Now play until you queen. King in front, key square, and only then the pawn.
ex.e09: Gligorić against Fischer, 1959. Only one move holds.
ex.e09.hint: Do not go to the seventh rank: there the white king takes the opposition. Stay on the eighth, in front of the pawn.
ex.e09.solution: 57...Kb8! Only then, when the white king comes up, Black takes the opposition: 58.Kc5 Kc7 or 58.Kb5 Kb7. That is what Fischer played, and the white king never reached the key squares a6, b6 and c6.
ex.e10: A position by Jan Drtina, 1908. The direct road does not work.
ex.e10.hint: The key squares are b5, c5 and d5. Through the centre the black king gets there first; try the other side of the pawn.
ex.e10.solution: 1.Kc2!, then 2.Kb3, 3.Kb4 and, with the opposition on c4, the king enters b5. Down the d-file the black king reaches c6, takes the opposition and draws.
ex.e12: Golombek against Pomar, 1946. The most stubborn defence is the corner.
ex.e12.hint: The black king wants h8, to be stalemated when the pawn checks. Take the king to h6 and advance the pawn only with the king beside it.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Kh6!, 1...Kh8, 2.g6, 2...Kg8, 3.g7 and, after 3...Kf7, 4.Kh7: the pawn queens. 1.Kf6 also wins, but after 1...Kh7 it has to come back with 2.Kf7 and 3.Kg6.
ex.e14: Maróczy against Marshall, Monte Carlo 1903. This time the pawn is yours, and the white king waits in the corner.
ex.e14.hint: The key squares of the g5-pawn are f3, g3 and h3. The pawn waits; the king moves first. And near the corner, before every move, check whether the white king still has a square.
ex.e14.solution: 58...Kg4! The king goes in front of the pawn, towards the key squares; 58...g4? and 58...Kh5? only draw. After 59.Kh2, 59...Kf3 (59...Kf4 and 59...Kh4 also work) and, after 60.Kh3, 60...g4+ (or 60...Kf4). With the white king back on h2, only 61...Kf2! wins: it takes g1 from the white king, and the pawn walks down with the king beside it. 61...g3+? and the other king moves let the win slip.
ex.e15: The pawns are blocked, and your king is further away than Black's. Find the winning move.
ex.e15.hint: A blocked pawn has key squares too. For your king they are the squares on the sixth rank beside the b6-pawn: a6, c6, d6 and e6. For the black king, the ones on the fifth: a5, c5, d5 and e5. Whoever gets there first wins, and the shortest road is the diagonal.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Kg3! and the king walks down the diagonal: 2.Kf4, 3.Ke5, 4.Kd5 and, after 4...Kc7, 5.Ke6 (5.Ke5 also works). With the king on a key square, it goes through d7 and c7 and wins the b6-pawn. 1.Kg3, 2.Kf4, 3.Ke5 and 4.Kd5 are all only moves: 1.Kg2? or 1.Kg1? waste a tempo and draw; 1.Kh3? and 1.Kh1? arrive late and even lose, because the black king reaches c5 or d5 first. The example comes from Jesús de la Villa's book.
ex.e16: Both kings are one step from the enemy pawn. Only one move does not lose. Find the winning move.
ex.e16.hint: It is mutual zugzwang: whoever has to move once the kings face the pawns loses his own. Attack e6 from a square that still leaves you a spare square for the next move.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Kd7! The king already eyes e6 and keeps d6 as a spare square. After 1...Kf5, 2.Kd6! Now Black is in zugzwang, and the black king has to leave f5; after 2...Kg6, 3.Kxe6 (3.Ke7 also wins). 1.Kd6?? straight away loses: 1...Kf5 and the zugzwang changes sides. Every other move loses too. Jesús de la Villa's example.
key.count: Every pawn has three key squares, two ranks in front of it: the square straight ahead and its two neighbours. If the white king reaches one of them, the pawn queens, whoever is to move.
key.averbakh: The white king is already on a key square, in front of the pawn. Now it moves forward using the opposition, always ahead of the pawn, up to the sixth rank: White wins.
key.opposition: A trap: taking the opposition out of habit only draws here. What wins is the white king stepping forward, beside the pawn, towards the key squares. The opposition is a means, not an end.
key.kamskyKramnik: Kamsky against Kramnik, Nice 2009, in a blindfold game: the black king stayed in front of the pawn, answered every white step, and the game ended in stalemate.
history: King and pawn against king is the most basic ending in chess, and it turns up at the end of many games: knowing whether it wins or draws tells you whether to trade everything off beforehand. It looks simple, but one wrong king step turns a win into a draw, and it has happened to champions. The great shortcut comes from the Russian Yuri Averbakh: instead of calculating, look for the key squares, the squares that guarantee the win once your king steps on them. He compared the king to a father crossing the street ahead of his child. In 1959, at the Candidates Tournament, the young Fischer saved half a point against Gligorić by finding the only king route that held the draw. And in 2009, playing blindfold, Kramnik drew against Kamsky by keeping his king firmly in front of the pawn.
practice: Now the real ending: king on d2, pawn on g2, and the black king waiting. Count the key squares, lead with the king and queen the pawn. Pick your pace and go.
step.t_count.hint2: For a pawn up to the fourth rank, there are three squares, side by side, on the same rank.
step.d_why: King on e6, a key square, and Black to move. Watch: it makes no difference who moves.
step.d_why.m1: 1...Kd8. The black king cannot stand still: d7, e7 and f7 belong to my king, and he has to step aside from the pawn.
step.d_why.m2: 2.Kf7. I take the square on the other side, next to e8. The black king never gets back in front of the pawn.
step.d_why.m3: 2...Kd7. He stays close, to the side, waiting for a slip.
step.d_why.m4: 3.e5. Now the pawn walks, protected: e6, e7 and e8 belong to my king, and Black cannot get in front.
step.d_why.m5: 3...Kd8. e7 and e8 are still guarded by my king; Black cannot get back in front of the pawn and can only wait to the side.
step.d_why.m6: 4.e6. The pawn goes on with the king beside it; next it reaches the seventh and then queens. With Black to move, the key square won just the same.
step.t_averbakh.hint2: Kings face to face, one square between them and his move: when he gives way to one side, where does yours advance?
step.d_averbakh: This is the example {{Averbakh|yuri-averbakh}} used. Watch the white king climb to the sixth rank without touching the pawn.
step.d_averbakh.m1: 1.Kc4! Kings face to face on the c-file, one square between them, Black to move: that is the opposition. Only this move wins.
step.d_averbakh.m2: 1...Kb6. The black king cannot stand still and has to give up one side. He went to b6.
step.d_averbakh.m3: 2.Kd5. I go in on the side he left, one step higher. From here he cannot push me back.
step.d_averbakh.m4: 2...Kc7. He comes back to the pawn's file, in front of my king.
step.d_averbakh.m5: 3.Kc5. The opposition again, now on the fifth, and again it is his move.
step.d_averbakh.m6: 3...Kd7. He gives way to the other side.
step.d_averbakh.m7: 4.Kb6. King on the sixth, ahead of the pawn: from here it queens, and the pawn has not even left c2.
part.kingFirst.title: The king goes first
part.kingFirst.summary: A pawn that advances too early gives away the draw. The king moves first.
step.t_early: The black king is on d6, watching the d2-pawn. Think: what does White do first to win, and where does he want to get to?
step.t_early.hint1: Two ranks ahead of the pawn are the squares that matter. Does the pawn need to move for the king to get there?
step.early: Until now the king was already close to the key squares. Now he has to reach them. The key squares of the d2-pawn are c4, d4 and e4. The king goes in front, like a father crossing the street with his child behind; the pawn waits, protected, until the king opens the way.
step.d_early: See what happens if White plays d4 straight away. The pawn moved two squares, and the key squares moved up with it.
step.d_early.m1: 1...Kd5. The black king stops in front of the pawn. The key squares are now c6, d6 and e6, and the white king is far from them.
step.d_early.m2: 2.Kd3. The white king comes close to the pawn.
step.d_early.m3: 2...Kd6. Black does not stay glued to the pawn: he steps back one square, on its file, and waits to see which way the white king goes.
step.d_early.m4: 3.Ke4. The white king tries to get through via d5 or f5.
step.d_early.m5: 3...Ke6! The only move that holds: kings face to face on the e-file, White to move, and the white king gets through neither d5 nor f5.
step.d_early.m6: 4.d5+. The pawn advances with check, but it does not help: the black king goes back in front of it.
step.d_early.m7: 4...Kd6. A draw. The pawn left too early, the key squares were out of the white king's reach, and Black defends as you will see in the next chapter.
step.t_kramnik.hint2: When the white king reaches the fifth rank, in front of the pawn, where must yours be to answer with the opposition?
step.d_backRank: Before {{Kramnik|vladimir-kramnik}}'s position, the same defence with the pawn further back. White king on e4, pawn on d4, Black to move.
step.d_backRank.m1: 1...Ke6! The only move that holds: the opposition on the e-file. The white king gets into neither d5 nor f5.
step.d_backRank.m2: 2.d5+. With no way in for the king, White pushes the pawn with check.
step.d_backRank.m3: 2...Kd6. The king goes back in front of the pawn, where it belongs.
step.d_backRank.m4: 3.Kd4. The white king comes behind the pawn and threatens to go up via c5 or e5.
step.d_backRank.m5: 3...Kd7. Straight back, on the pawn's file. If the white king goes to c5 or e5, Black answers on the same file as him, on the seventh (4...Kc7 or 4...Ke7), and takes the opposition.
part.knightPawn.title: The knight pawn
part.knightPawn.summary: With the black king in the corner, the white king's natural square gives stalemate. Leave him a square.
step.t_knight: The goal is to win. The b6-pawn is close to queening, and the black king has hidden in the corner. Where does the white king go, and what must not happen?
step.t_knight.hint1: Before choosing the king's square, count the squares left for the black king.
step.knightTrap: So far the rule worked for the centre pawns. The knight pawn has a trap. 1.Kc7 looks natural, but it is stalemate: a7 belongs to the pawn, b7 and b8 to the white king, and the black king has no move. With a knight pawn, the corner is the last defence.
step.knightRule: The way out is to leave the black king a square: the white king goes to c6, and the pawn moves only when the king is beside it. With the knight pawn further back, on the fifth, the same care applies.
step.d_knight: Watch the technique: the king gives room, the pawn moves, and only then does the king close the queening square.
step.d_knight.m1: 1.Kc6! The only winning move. The black king keeps b8 to breathe, and there is no stalemate.
step.d_knight.m3: 2.b7! Now it is time: the pawn advances protected by the king, and the black king only has a7.
step.d_knight.m4: 2...Ka7. Forced, and the black king has left the front of the pawn.
step.d_knight.m5: 3.Kc7! It guards b8, the queening square, and the black king still has a6: no stalemate.
step.d_knight.m6: 3...Ka6. There is no way back to the corner.
step.d_knight.m7: 4.b8=Q. The pawn queens. The white king always stayed beside the pawn, without taking the black king's last square.
step.knightMove: Now with the g6-pawn. White to play and win; the black king is on h8.
step.knightMove.hint: Bring the king close to the pawn, but leave g8 free for the black king.
step.knightMove.done: Pawn on the seventh, king on f7: the queening square is yours, and the black king still has h6. No stalemate.
part.anyRoute.title: Any route will do
part.anyRoute.summary: Any key square will do. If the black king guards some, the white king goes in by the others.
step.t_route: The goal is to win. The black king is running to the d3-pawn. Which key square can he not reach in time, and which way does your king go?
step.t_route.hint1: The key squares of the d3-pawn are c5, d5 and e5.
step.t_route.hint2: One of them is on your side of the board.
step.route: Until now the king went in from the front. But the three key squares are worth the same. The black king runs to guard d5 and e5; the white king goes by the c5 side and, at the end, uses the opposition. 1.Kb2, or any other move, loses a tempo and already draws: every move counts.
step.d_route: Watch the white king go round on the queenside.
step.d_route.m1: 1.Kb3! The only winning move: it is the shortest way to c4, and from there to c5.
step.d_route.m2: 1...Ke6. The black king comes to the centre to guard d5.
step.d_route.m4: 2...Kd6. Now he guards c5 and d5 at the same time.
step.d_route.m5: 3.Kd4! Kings face to face on the d-file, one square between them, Black to move: the opposition. It is also the only move.
step.d_route.m6: 3...Kc6. The black king has to give up one side. He chose c6, to guard c5.
step.d_route.m7: 4.Ke5. A key square, on the side he left. From here the pawn queens.
step.routeMove: Your turn. The black king guards c5; look for another key square.
step.routeMove.hint: Kings face to face, one square between them, and his move.
step.routeMove.done: King on d5, in front of the pawn, with the opposition. You went in on the other side, and it worked just the same.
part.blocked.title: Blocked pawns
part.blocked.summary: With the pawns blocked, each king has its own key squares, and whoever gets there first wins.
step.t_blocked: The pawns are blocked and cannot move any more. Who reaches the other's pawn first, and by which route?
step.t_blocked.hint1: For your king, the squares that matter are on the sixth rank, near the f6-pawn.
step.t_blocked.hint2: Count the moves of both kings; the shortest way is hardly ever straight.
step.blocked: Until now only one side had a pawn; now the opponent has one too, blocked in front of yours. The white king's key squares are on the sixth rank next to the f6-pawn, up to three files on each side: c6, d6, e6, g6 and h6. The black king's are on the fifth: c5, d5, e5, g5 and h5. The king that steps on one first wins the other's pawn. The shortest way to d6 is the diagonal: 1.Kb4, 2.Kc5 and 3.Kd6.
step.d_blocked: The white king is on a3, far away; the black one on h8. Count with me.
step.d_blocked.m1: 1.Kb4! The only winning move. Along the diagonal the king reaches d6 in three moves; 1.Kb3 only draws, and 1.Ka4 even loses.
step.d_blocked.m2: 1...Kg7. The black king comes close to the f6-pawn.
step.d_blocked.m3: 2.Kc5. Also the only move: one more step down the diagonal, and next comes d6.
step.d_blocked.m4: 2...Kf8. He keeps an eye on e7, so the white king cannot go in there.
step.d_blocked.m5: 3.Kd6. A key square. The black king only guards e6 and e7 together from f7, and then White forces him to give one up: the f6-pawn falls. That is what you will play now.
step.blockedMove: Now you finish it. White to play and win the f6-pawn.
step.blockedMove.hint: The black king guards e6 and e7. Place your king so that he has to let go of one of them.
step.blockedMove.done: The f6-pawn fell and yours is protected: it is king and pawn against king, with your king in front. You already know the technique.
part.mutualZugzwang.title: Mutual zugzwang
part.mutualZugzwang.summary: When each king attacks the other's pawn, whoever is to move loses. Get there with the opponent to move.
step.t_zz: Blocked pawns again, and both kings are close to the enemy pawn. Your king can attack d5 right now. Should it?
step.t_zz.hint1: Both kings want the same thing: to attack the other's pawn and guard their own.
step.t_zz.hint2: Think about who will be to move when both kings arrive.
step.zz: In the previous chapter, one king got there before the other. Here both arrive together. Kc5 against Ke4: each king attacks the other's pawn and guards its own. Whoever has to move here loses the pawn. This is mutual zugzwang, and what decides is reaching this position with the other side to move.
step.d_zzWrong: See what happens if White goes to c5 straight away.
step.d_zzWrong.m1: 1...Ke4! The zugzwang position is on the board, and White is the one to move.
step.d_zzWrong.m2: 2.Kb5. Any white king move lets go of the d4-pawn.
step.d_zzWrong.m3: 2...Kxd4. The pawn has fallen, and now Black is the one who wins.
step.zzMove: Your turn. Only one move does not lose.
step.zzMove.hint: Attack d5 from a square that is not c5 yet, and keep c5 for later.
step.zzMove.done: 1.Kc6 kept c5 in reserve. When the black king reached e4, you were the one to step into c5, and the zugzwang was on his side.
